newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada confirms Chile free trade deal now agreed.
newsitem.headline: Canada confirms Chile free trade deal now agreed.

text.p: Canadian International Trade Minister Art Eggleton confirmed on Thursday that Canada and Chile had finally reached a free trade agreement, a deal the two countries hope will foreshadow Chile's entry into NAFTA.

Eggleton had planned to announce the agreement 2-1/2 hours earlier but at the last minute had said Chile had asked Canada to reconsider a couple of items. Subsequently Chilean Finance Minister Eduardo Aninat announced the deal in Santiago.
"The hiccup is over," Eggleton told a news conference. "I am happy to announce a free trade agreement with Chile."
Canada's chief negotiator with Chile, Keith Christie, said that the deal will allow Canadians to invest in Chile without depositing 30 percent of their investment with Chile's central bank.
Chile will however retain the right for a limited period to require the 30 percent deposits for Canadian credits or loans, he added.
"Under current law, the central bank of Chile has the right to impose the 30 percent reserve requirement on almost all forms of capital inflows and outflows into Chile," Christie said.

"In practice in the last couple of years it has chosen to impose that requirement. What we've done in the agreement is ensure that we have a freeze on current practice. That is, the bulk of central bank authority to impose these controls...has now been frozen. It can never be applied on Canadian investors. It can only be applied for a maximum of two years on investments that take the form of loans from abroad."

"If a company brings in its own capital, if it uses domestic capital or uses its own capital to buy shares on the stock market, those forms of investment will no longer be subject to the threat of the 30 percent reserve requirement," Christie added.

He said current practice is for the 30 percent requirement to be applied for the first 12 months of the term of a loan. The agreement with Canada allows for this to go to 24 months, Christie said, but said Chile assured Canada it does not intend to boost the time period.
Eggleton said Chilean President Eduardo Frei and Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien would sign "an agreement of all the details" in Ottawa on Monday but the final legal text would be signed later.
He hoped that it could become law, after parliamentary approval, sometime during the northern hemisphere's spring.

Current bilateral trade of about C$665 million annually could easily double under the agreement, Eggleton said, adding that Canada had C$7 billion of investments either made or planned in the South American country.
"I think we're opening up a great new marketing opportunity here," he said.
Durum wheat, representing 35 percent of Canadian agricultural exports to Chile, will gain immediate duty-free access during the April-November export season.

An 11 percent duty on milling wheat, used for bread, will be phased out in 17 years -- the same period as for Argentine wheat -- but in eight years the two sides will consider speeding this provision up.
